summary:
CardioScan Space Health brings focused cardiac-monitoring technology into a broader workspace for astronaut wellbeing. We developed a web application that combines ECG visualization, daily check-ins, personal history, and explainable health indicators, building on our portable CardioScan hardware project.

Crews can record pulse, sleep, stress, activity, symptoms, and optional measurements such as blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, and glucose. A locally deployable machine-learning model generates an illustrative score, while the interface shows the contributing factors. Pending check-ins remain on the device during connection failures and synchronize when the server becomes available.

We use NASA OSDR glucose observations to anchor synthetic training examples and preserve historical ISS radiation measurements as separate environmental context. Our innovation connects a compact cardiac-monitoring device, local processing, and transparent mission-health observations in one workflow. The intended impact is clearer information for crews and medical teams when connectivity and space are limited. The space-health adaptation is a research prototype, not a validated diagnostic system.
details:
CardioScan Space Health builds on our existing portable cardiac-monitoring project, which our team is taking through clinical testing in Kazakhstan. The space-health adaptation extends that foundation into an application combining ECG visualization, daily wellbeing observations, personal history, and understandable calculations.

The hardware architecture uses an ADS1293 acquisition stage and ESP32 to deliver ECG samples to a local CardioScan application through supported USB or Wi-Fi connections. The monitor displays channels, tracks missing samples, stores recordings locally, and requests analysis after at least ten seconds of signal. A clearly labeled synthetic mode supports demonstrations without connected hardware.

A separate daily-score model processes 23 features using median imputation and a 300-tree Random Forest regressor. It approximates an explicit rubric covering pulse, sleep, wellbeing, activity, symptoms, and available optional measurements. Users see factor contributions and coverage. Urgent symptom rules take priority over the aggregate score.

NASA OSD-575 supplies observed glucose values that anchor synthetic training examples. Historical ISS RadLab readings provide separate environmental context. Neither source establishes clinical accuracy for the astronaut score.

We developed the interface with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and IndexedDB. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, and PostgreSQL; research models use NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn.

Our approach connects portable hardware, local cardiac processing, and broader mission observations. Core ECG processing does not require cloud inference, and check-ins survive temporary server disconnections. We considered limited connectivity, equipment size, incomplete readings, signal quality, privacy, and explainability. Our intended impact is a clearer history for crews and medical specialists.
